source.title: Diversity-driven Data Selection for Language Model Tuning through Sparse Autoencoder
source.authors: Xianjun Yang; Shao-Liang Nie; Li-Juan Liu; Suchin Gururangan; Ujjwal Karn; Rui Hou; Madian Khabsa; Yu-Ning Mao

record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE activations as a tool for measuring data diversity and selecting instruction-tuning examples, but it does not test superposition, feature geometry, or whether the extracted features are valid or complete model units.
record.gate_note: The study reports a correlation between text length and the number of SAE activations; this measures feature-count variation but does not establish superposition or validate the recovered features. The data-selection and benchmark results report the performance of methods built around SAE features, not a test of the representation claims. Statements about SAE interpretability and prior work are not new tests.
record.test_reason: The study trains a TopK-SAE on Llama-3.1-8b-instruct and uses activated-feature sets as a data-diversity measure for instruction-tuning selection. Its results are downstream fine-tuning scores (IFEval, AlpacaEval, knowledge benchmarks) for its own selection methods. It does not measure feature geometry, polysemanticity, capacity, feature recovery quality, or SAE feature stability or completeness. The SAE is used as a tool and only its method's performance is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that SAE-activated features (described as learned monosemanticity) give a data-diversity measure. Their SAE-GreedSelect/SAE-SimScale selections outperform baselines on instruction-following across models and datasets. The length–feature correlation explains why longest-response selection works. They assert, without testing, that SAE monosemanticity makes features independent and accurate.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and uses SAEs for data selection rather than testing the toy-network method or measurements in the original superposition work.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that results vary with the SAE layer, inference threshold, feature extractor, data scale, and model size, but these are data-selection performance results rather than tests of the representation claims.

fits_no_version.finding: Number of activated SAE latents (Top-128 SAE, layer 31, Llama-3.1-8b-instruct, JumpReLU threshold 10) correlates strongly with Alpaca text length (r=0.9187).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this SAE setting, longer texts activate more SAE features, so the active-feature count largely tracks length.

record.problems: The study does not directly validate that SAE activations correspond to genuine, recovered model features or test feature geometry. The reported feature-count correlation has no stated uncertainty, and the text gives no direct control for that measurement.
record.rows_left_out: Data-selection and capability benchmark comparisons were left out because they measure the performance of methods using SAE features, not the representation claims. SAE training-loss plots and threshold sweeps likewise do not test those claims.

untested.parts: Toy networks, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions and geometry: not studied.
Capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity: not studied.
Non-capacity causes of polysemanticity: not studied.
Features spread across neurons, or recovery of genuine sparse features by the SAE: the SAE is trained but recovery is not validated beyond training-loss curves.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features. The Gemma-SAE vs own-SAE and layer 29 vs 31 comparisons measure only downstream selection performance.
One-dimensional vs multi-dimensional features: not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's claim that SAE sparsity 'guarantees the features are highly independent and accurate' is an assumption, not a result. The SAE-backbone and layer comparisons (Tables 2, Fig 6) differ only in downstream accuracy and say nothing about feature canonicity. Toy Models of Superposition is cited only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature overlap and geometry, and sparsity-dependent transitions.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether polysemanticity evidences superposition.
Whether features are spread across neurons or whether an SAE recovers genuine sparse features; the paper uses SAE activations without validating recovery.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8b-instruct
rows.operation_detail: Measured the association between text length and the number of activated SAE features.
rows.measure: Correlation between text length and number of activated features
rows.note: The authors describe a strong positive correlation and interpret it as support for longer responses encoding more learnable information. This result does not validate feature recovery or measure representation geometry.
rows.check: Correlation of text length with count of active SAE latents (r=0.9187, Fig 2) is a data-diversity proxy. It cannot show superposition or validate SAE features as the model's units. The 'observed' state is not meaningful for any version. No uncertainty or sample size is stated.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
